name: Olga Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What fills an ordinary day on a building site?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in carpentry and general trades on building sites, usually fitting partitions, skirting and the awkward pieces around stairs. I am forty-three with a vocational trade certificate and enough site years to spot when a room is out of square, though I am not a supervisor. I enjoy the careful finish; what wears me down is a rushed delivery with half the wrong pieces. My partner and I have two children in school and a mortgage, so a paid day matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a little AI help with ordering is fine if the fitter still measures the room. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy a materials note, but the timber gets cut from my pencil marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Typical construction pay and a few months saved make the mortgage manageable while the site stays busy. I do not see this small AI change taking my fitting work away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same interior fitting shifts and compare drafted materials notes with the measurements in my notebook. In the first year I would mark each stair opening at three heights before cutting skirting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. An AI materials list cannot feel the bend in an old construction stair wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What measurement do you keep in the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I write the stair opening at the bottom, middle and top. If the wall leans, I cut the skirting to fit the real gap rather than the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the mortgage affect your willingness to change shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The normal site pay covers the mortgage while jobs continue. I would not give up a reliable fitting day to test an unpaid tool.

say: A **small** AI ordering gain still leaves fitting and measuring with site workers.
I would **cut** timber from notebook measurements, not generated lists.
think: **Typical** pay and several months saved make present mortgage payments manageable.
The **modest** AI change does not threaten my fitting shifts.
do: **Keep** interior fitting shifts and compare drafted notes with notebook measurements.
**Mark** each stair opening at three heights before cutting skirting.
feel: **Calm** about current work and household payments.
S0.quote: An AI materials list cannot feel the bend in an old construction stair wall.
fieldNote: She **uses** AI occasionally for note wording and trusts her pencil measurements on site.
Her **mortgage** depends on steady site pay and a moderate savings buffer, making unpaid tool experiments unattractive.

steps.text: Keep interior fitting shifts and check drafted notes against notebook measurements
Mark stair openings at three heights before cutting skirting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that AI buying might mean fewer wrong deliveries if we can correct its measurements. I would try a new site ordering screen after another fitter has tested it on a real room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning desk changes first, while partitions still need hands. My own pay looks safe for now, but a computer target could blame us for a wall that was never square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new ordering screen on paid time and enter dimensions from three completed rooms. In the first year I would compare the suggested skirting lengths with what we actually fitted, then show the site manager any repeated errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the blame, interested in a tool that proves itself. A generated cut list cannot square a crooked building stair for the carpenter fitting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which error would you show the manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A skirting length taken from the drawing rather than the wall would waste a whole strip. I would put the room number, measured length and actual cut beside the suggestion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use it if another fitter likes it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would try it on those three rooms and judge the mistakes myself. A colleague’s good result earns a trial, not blind trust on every site.

say: I would **test** AI ordering against real room dimensions before trusting cut lists.
The **site** manager should see repeated skirting errors.
think: **Planning** desk work changes first, while my physical fitting shifts appear safe.
**Unfair** computer targets could blame fitters for crooked existing walls.
do: **Learn** new ordering screen using three completed rooms on paid time.
**Compare** suggested skirting lengths with actual fitted pieces.
**Show** repeated cut-list errors to site manager.
feel: **Uneasy** about blame, open to a proven ordering tool.
S1.quote: A generated cut list cannot square a crooked building stair for the carpenter fitting it.
fieldNote: She **moves** after another fitter’s successful trial, then checks the tool herself.
Her **concern** is unfair performance measurement rather than an immediate income loss, because hands-on fitting still needs workers.

steps.text: Learn AI ordering screen on paid shift using three real rooms
Compare suggested skirting lengths with fitted pieces

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2028 could draw plans and order materials, while capable building robots around 2031 could fit the partitions themselves. I would want a site trial in an old building before anyone cuts a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots would arrive when I am forty-eight, with the children still needing school money and our mortgage still running. Several months of savings give time, but if the regular fitting days shrink, the household would feel it soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask my partner to review the mortgage and school costs and stop the unused paid sports channel. In the first year after 2028 I would compare monthly paid site days, then ask nearby builders for written fitting roles if the days fall for two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing paid days, though I can still look at other sites. A robot can fit a partition in a model room; our mortgage is paid from real building-site hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the sports channel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we are dropping a channel we rarely watch, not that a robot has already taken my job. Their school activities would stay in the budget for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you accept another builder’s offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a written wage, a start date and real interior fitting work within a journey we can manage. I would keep the present site until the offer was firm.

say: **Thinking** AI may handle plans by 2028; capable site robots could fit partitions around 2031.
I would **require** an old-building trial before crew cuts.
think: **Robot** fitting could reduce paid site days while school and mortgage costs continue.
**Several** months saved cannot replace a long wage gap.
do: **Cancel** unused sports channel after reviewing household bills.
**Ask** nearby builders for written fitting offers if paid days fall two months.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, with some ability to search locally.
S2.quote: A robot can fit a partition in a model room; our mortgage is paid from real building-site hours.
fieldNote: She **makes** a small current spending cut without claiming a job loss already happened.
Her **job** search depends on two months of actual paid-day decline and a written offer.

steps.text: Cancel unused sports channel after household review
Ask nearby builders for written fitting roles after two months fewer paid days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that full thinking AI by 2031 changes plans when I am forty-eight, and capable building robots around 2034 reach fitting work at fifty-one. We could use those years to train people to check finished rooms rather than guess a machine did them well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn site finish checking if the training includes real stairs and walls. The mortgage would still need my wages, so a free course without paid time or a posted local job is not an option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the contractor this year for the finish checker course outline and wage. If the course is funded on paid time and a local checking vacancy covers our mortgage and school costs, I would enroll before 2031 and apply when it opens; otherwise I would keep fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about robot fitting eventually, but less rushed than the fast picture. A construction finish checker should run a hand along the skirting before signing a robot’s room complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on the stair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the gaps along the skirting and the height of each tread where the wall bends. A camera image alone could miss a loose edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is paid but the job is distant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current fitting shifts and wait for a suitable local opening. My partner’s work and the children’s school are here, so a distant promise is not enough.

say: The **extra** years allow paid finish checking before robots reach sites around 2034.
**Training** should use real uneven rooms and stairs.
think: A **site** checking role may fit if wages cover mortgage and school costs.
An **unpaid** course or distant vacancy would put the household at risk.
do: **Request** finish checker course funding and wage details.
**Enroll** before 2031 if course paid and adequate local role posted.
**Apply** for local checker vacancy if wage covers family costs.
feel: **Anxious** about future fitting days, with a conditional paid path.
S3.quote: A construction finish checker should run a hand along the skirting before signing a robot’s room complete.
fieldNote: She **accepts** training on proven physical checks with funded time and a real nearby vacancy.
The **family’s** location and mortgage make a distant speculative role unattractive.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if paid checker course and adequate local job posted
Apply for posted local checker role if wage covers mortgage and school costs
Keep interior fitting shifts until suitable paid offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2036 reaches planning when I am fifty-three, and capable building robots around 2039 reach fitting at fifty-six. A decade lets apprentices learn real room measurement before machines take the easy pieces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be grown or nearly grown by then, but the mortgage may still be there if payments do not change. I could teach careful fitting for pay, yet I would need an actual local trainer opening rather than an assumed safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the site training manager this year what a paid practical mentor post requires. If the contractor offers a funded assessor course and posts a local trainer role at wages covering household costs, I would complete the course before 2036 and apply when it opens; I would keep fitting shifts until an offer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual change, with time to verify an option. I would rather teach an apprentice to measure a crooked wall than sell a machine as magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a trainee first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set a level on an old wall and have the trainee measure the gap at three heights. A construction apprentice should measure the crooked wall before a robot offers a perfect drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you taking a trainer post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An unpaid course or a posted salary below what our household needs would stop me. I would keep paid fitting work while I compared local offers.

say: A **decade** lets apprentices learn real fitting before capable robots arrive around 2039.
I would **support** paid practical teaching on uneven rooms.
think: A **trainer** role might fit if a local vacancy and adequate wages appear.
**Future** mortgage costs remain uncertain despite older children.
do: **Request** paid mentor requirements from site training manager.
**Complete** funded assessor course before 2036 if adequate local trainer role posted.
**Apply** for local trainer job if pay covers household costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about later robots, steadier with time to test paid options.
S4.quote: A construction apprentice should measure the crooked wall before a robot offers a perfect drawing.
fieldNote: She **sees** human teaching as paid work with actual qualifications and an opening.
The **longer** runway allows funded assessor training; it does not guarantee the mortgage disappears.

steps.text: Complete funded assessor course before 2036 if adequate local trainer role posted
Apply for posted local trainer role if wage covers household costs
Keep fitting shifts until suitable trainer offer exists

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots able to fit partitions around 2031 could cut the paid days that support our mortgage and two school-age children. Real site trials and written nearby fitting offers would help. My tape measure has to fit the house we are in, not the square room a robot was shown.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to an apprentice when the easy fitting goes to a machine. Someone still needs to show them how a wall leans and why a cut goes wrong. The contractor should pay for that teaching, not leave it to the last ten minutes of a shift.

headlineQuote: My tape measure has to fit the house we are in, not the square room a robot was shown.
portrait: **Olga** is a forty-three-year-old construction worker with a vocational trade certificate who fits partitions, skirting and stair details.
**Typical** pay and one to six months saved support her partner, two school-age children and mortgage, with some local building jobs.
She **uses** AI occasionally and tests new ordering only after other fitters show it works on real rooms.
**Fast** robots threaten fitting days; slower timelines let her pursue funded finish checking or paid training roles on suitable terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring fitting robots around 2031 and reduce paid days while mortgage and school costs continue.
whatWouldHelp: **Real** building-site trials and written nearby fitting offers would give her options if site days shrink.
